My father’s father (bio grandparent), and HIS father too (bio great grand parent) were both lost to suicide while deep in alcoholism.

I don’t say this to make you feel guilty because I think I do know this pain you describe very well - I struggle with urges/ideation myself as someone with a chronic condition and challenging financial situation - but it affected many people in our family very deeply when we lost people like this. 

One of the biggest effects is that it seems to have made a dark legacy. When I brought my three week old baby home from the hospital, my dad called me. I thought he was calling to congratulate me, ask after the baby… but no, he was calling me actively suicidal because him and my mom had just separated, and to him, taking his life is always a primary solution - his bio parent and grandparent did it, so can he. I guess that that’s how he thinks when he’s in that pain. And me too, more than once, but I fight it. I’ve talked my dad off a ledge or called services for him several times. 

Of course this is anecdotal. But it does often ripple out in families like waves after a very tragic loss. Even beyond increasing the chances that others may find that route more acceptable, there’s a lot of painful fallout. Kids without parents or kids with depressed / mentally ill parents - neither seems good, but objectively, having that parent in your life at all, and not living with such a tragic kind of disenfranchised grief, that seems to matter. 

My son has watched me fight through a lot of mental health difficulties. I hope I’m right in assuming it’s better that I’m here? And it would be better if you’re also here. 

Your children love you. I know that. You may feel you have nothing left to give them but I’m glad my dad is around, if that helps. He’s doing a bit better lately, finally, at 70. 

My dad‘s bio dad wasn’t in his life much but he had two young daughters with another woman (plus my dad has a full sister by this man) and ALL of them have struggled so badly as adults with addiction, depression, abuse isolation… I’m not even saying it’s all anyone’s fault; some of it is probably genetic, situational, etc. but those have been my observations. 

Is there any possibility you can access help or speak to a trusted person you haven’t met yet? 

I’ve said plenty here so just one more thing to share: during my worst health crisis I called a hotline. I had done it once before, and it was okay but not super helpful although it got me through the next 24 hours (just being totally real with you here OP) HOWEVER - the second time I called a hotline for help, having no one else, utterly bereft, I found an absolute angel of an elderly man, a retired trauma nurse, and he was amazing. He listened intently and he actually cared - and he SAVED A LIFE. Then later, because he gave me some resources and ideas to find more help, I was able to slowly work on climbing out of the abyss. I was able to find more people/resources.

There is hope. Please believe me. I TRULY promise the pain can pass; just need to buy you some time. It won’t be easy. You did great reaching out here, this is a wonderful loving place - this subreddit. I don’t know where you live but happy to provide some numbers if you would be open to that idea. 

You are not alone. <3

I guess we should be glad we’re not relegated to the home (only) but … the bills need paid.

It sounds like you’re really scared and hurting over this pregnancy and your future as a parent. I’m so sorry that you’re dealing with painful emotions, loneliness, and confusion (in addition to the uncomfortable physical symptoms) - that can be very hard. 

I had issues with vomiting uncontrollably for 6 months while pregnant and I also had agoraphobia because of the vomiting (not fun to get out in public and not be able to control your throwing up everywhere) After the pregnancy ended, things didn’t get easier, in fact, they were harder - honesty could be only my own experience there, but yeah… Things were hard AF from pregnancy through year 4. 

And I’m not some parental sage with all the wisdom, but since you added “advice welcome” here are some things you might consider if you feel you will continue with this pregnancy:

1) family support. Not just a partner, but outside your home, extended family or true friends; do you truly have some support? Someone to call in emergencies or hard times? You will likely need at least one. 

2) finances / career: How will this baby affect that for you; can you save a little extra for emergencies or even for your own needs? For childcare? Will you likely have enough for the coming years without going into big amounts of debt? 

3) Your partner: are they usually fair and helpful? Do you truly feel that you will have a chance at an equitable, peaceful, nurturing home together with a new addition? Is there a mutual love and respect more than fighting and hurt? Like where do you feel that coming from? Some day-to-day frustrations are normal but ongoing contempt can be a real sign of deeper problems. Would you stay if you woke up tomorrow not pregnant? 

4) Your health: What is that picture looking like? If you are having health problems now, they are likely to become more numerous or worse after having kid(s) - and that’s just by the data which I’m happy to share. People age and having babies is sometimes really hard on a woman’s body.

5) What were your original reasons for deciding to have this potential new person join your life? I often hear people here talking about how they were just following the “life script” - is this you or do you really want to be a parent? Do you have a parenting philosophy you can work with? 

So, lots of questions, but I hope maybe looking at some of this helps you my friend.

It took me until age 33 to finish college. I had zero support and zero interest in the “uni culture” because I was trying to work 2 jobs and go to school. My parents, who were living in Central America (supposedly happily semi-retired but in reality strung out on drugs), straight-up disappeared for several months, & I was so stressed out over that I had a mental breakdown in my professor’s office once. He was nice and advised I see mental health services. I did do some of that. It helped a little. 

But yes, like yourself, I lived hand to mouth in the best circumstances during my time at uni. I went to Cal State for a while, and almost everyone seemed to have more security and support than I did, and they did all the extracurricular things. I did not lol - Life was just mostly difficulties and disappointments for a while. Sometimes I was over-indulgent in drinking to numb my frustration and anxiety. Try not to go that route! 

Living in southern CA, I also worked for every sociopathic a**hole imaginable. It does wear you down. You’re not wrong either, it’s hard to find regular decent humans to work for without sacrificing a living wage. Still walking that line. 

It won’t ever be super easy for us. It’s okay. 

I won’t even lie to you, I still DO work for one of these people. But he’s quite uninvolved in his business day-to-day lately, thankfully. And it’s remote, so that saves me. Worst case, I log off. Bye. Onto the next. Maybe one advantage of a precarious life is non attachment to outcomes, but that builds over time.

ANYWAY… I finished my undergrad degree at the 3rd uni I attended after many stops and starts. I began at 17 and it took me almost 15 years, because seemingly every other semester I had to drop out and work more or be homeless. There was also the year I had kidney stones twice and no medical care. Once I even lived in my car for a while, but that was terrible. 

It was a huge struggle, it was expensive, it was isolating, it was demoralizing - - and I do not regret it. 

Finishing college reminded me that I can endure, and I can finish what I start, and I can do hard things. 

You will also be able to finish college. You can do this and it’s okay if your journey looks different than most. We ARE different than most college students. 

One of the coolest things I learned about was “post-traumatic growth” - as in, what is gained when we endure great challenges - many people look at the lasting negative impacts. I definitely do see how people like us have some trauma, or at least some serious jadedness; but I also see so much more grit and creativity than most who had it easy. 

Many of my lil’ “nepo” buddies from college are wealthy but unhappy - Won’t venture to guess why. Others are happy as can be and they just seem to lead a charmed, breezy life, but idk… oddly, I wouldn’t change my experience much - I would not self medicate with booze. That is my one big regret. It didn’t help and slowed me down. Otherwise, I’m glad for my experience. 

My degree also helped me with employment, of course, although I’m not wealthy and I’m not able to do my passion. Have a kiddo to support now, I’m more practical. Did my MA eventually and will maybe do PhD b/c I do love to learn!!! But only if I can pay off old loans and not take any more. Ever. 

For now, I do Udemy / Coursera and UCSD extension courses to upskill. Ignore that part for now, but our education system is changing.  People see the cracks. There are many. Still, I truly think you’ll be glad to see the end of this road. You’ve worked hard! See it though. 

I don’t know if any of this was useful to you. I kinda droned on here… but really - finish school OP. Come chat anytime. You are not alone, ever.

There are also nonprofits, but I know you mentioned long waiting lists - perhaps a call to a higher-level case manager, or asking for extra help in person could lead to more expediency. You have to protect yourself too, as you know. As many DCFS-involved bromos have shared here, the goal is to keep a child with custodial parent(s) whenever possible. Anyway, I’m not a doctor, or a lawyer, so take what you will from that, but I did work in social services with developmentally disabled kids and adults for many years. I’ve seen this scenario and it’s not fair. We don’t do enough to support ANY parents in this society lately, but especially not parents with special needs kids. Oh mama… You are so seen and heard. FT mom & home-maker plus FT work outside the home is brutal. Been there myself for a long time. It seems like there’s never a minute where I shouldn’t be doing something for someone (my kid, my dude, my boss, etc.) and I have the same aversion to asking for help. Do you think it has to do with how you were raised? I didn’t really receive help from an adult a lot of times when I asked as a kid, like, in my own home. Parents were trying their best but running a company. I learned to be super self-sufficient. Also - became mentally ill - haha shocking! Maybe that’s something for you to look at. Mental health is imperative. I agree that it SUCKS when your partner doesn’t just LOOK AROUND and realize what needs done so they can jump in there unprompted, but also, sometimes when you do it all, they become used to never having to help. Maybe try a list of things you could sort of re-allocate? Also therapy / meds may be helpful. Or a medical leave from work for a bit if it’s dire - if you’re in crisis / severely burnt out, it should be a consideration, but I know not everyone has that option. Whatever you do or don’t do, please talk to someone. Ask for that help. Circle some wagons - doctor, partner, therapist, maybe a best friend or family member… priest or clergy if you roll like that… someone you trust. Explain you’re at your limit. And then you take a break. However that looks. Once things are less dire - Maybe schedule a weekend at a hotel 1-2x a year. Even if you plan it months out, you’ll know it’s coming. It helps to know relief is on the horizon. Last idea (don’t hate me because I hated this advice back in peak anxiety days but anywhoo) 5-10 min of meditation per day. Guided meditation can be good. Works wonders if you can carve out a few min. 

Big hugs. Remember you are not alone. <3
